topic: The Physics of Pi: Colliding Blocks and Number Theory
target_audience: Undergraduate physics or computer science students with a basic grasp of mechanics

sections.title: The Hook: Counting Collisions
sections.content: Introduce the counter-intuitive phenomenon: when two blocks slide on a frictionless surface and collide, the total number of collisions between the blocks and a wall encodes the digits of Pi. Frame it as a 'digital mystery' where simple physics generates complex geometry.
sections.example: A small block (mass m) and a large block (mass 100^N * m) sliding toward a wall.

sections.title: Prerequisite Physics: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Establish the foundational mechanics: Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and kinetic energy. Use a graphical split-screen showing vector arrows for velocity to explain why the blocks switch directions upon impact.
sections.example: Visualizing two billiard balls: one stationary, one moving, showing the transfer of velocity vectors.

sections.title: The Phase Space Mapping
sections.content: Introduce the 'Phase Space' concept. Instead of 1D movement, represent the system as a single point in 2D space (x, y coordinates representing velocities). Collisions become 'bounces' off the walls of a geometric shape (a wedge or hyper-rectangle).
sections.example: An animation of a ball bouncing inside a triangular wedge where the angle of the wedge is related to the mass ratio of the blocks.

sections.title: The Geometric Bridge: Why Pi?
sections.content: Explain that the number of collisions is equivalent to the number of times a straight line (the trajectory in phase space) crosses the boundaries of the wedge. The total count converges to Pi because the geometry of the phase space 'unfolds' into a circle.
sections.example: A diagram showing the 'unfolding' method: reflecting the trajectory repeatedly to reveal a perfect circular arc corresponding to the angle of reflection.

sections.title: Conclusion & Visualization
sections.content: Summarize the result: As the mass of the large block grows by powers of 100, the count of collisions provides successive digits of Pi (e.g., 100^0 = 3, 100^1 = 31, 100^2 = 314). Conclude by linking discrete physical events to continuous mathematical constants.
sections.example: A 'collision meter' animation: As the heavy block gets larger (1, 100, 10,000), the collision counter ticks: 3... 31... 314.
